title: Coffee Knowledge 1: Espresso Foundations
summary: Most coffee drinks in an Australian café start with espresso. You will learn what espresso is, how cafés build drinks from it, and why every new barista must learn the café's own recipe.

blocks.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Most coffee drinks in an Australian café start with espresso. You will learn what espresso is, how cafés build drinks from it, and why every new barista must learn the café's own recipe.

items.prompt: Which coffee drinks do you know?
Have you watched a barista make espresso?
Why can the same drink taste different in two cafés?

blocks.title: 1. Espresso Is a Brewing Method
paragraphs: Espresso is not one special bean. It is a way to make coffee. A machine pushes hot water through finely ground coffee under pressure. The result is a small, strong drink called an espresso shot. A café can use different beans and roast levels for espresso. The word espresso tells us about the brewing method, not the country, bean, or roast. This is an important difference. A dark-roasted bean is not automatically espresso, and a lighter-roasted bean can also be used in an espresso machine.

images.alt: English lesson illustration for Coffee Knowledge 1: Espresso Foundations scene 1: A trainee watches espresso flow from a professional machine into a small cup.

items.prompt: What does the word espresso describe?
items.answer: It describes a brewing method that uses hot water, fine coffee grounds, and pressure.

blocks.title: 2. One Base, Many Drinks
paragraphs: The espresso shot is the base of many Australian café drinks. A short black is espresso by itself. A long black adds hot water. A flat white, latte, and cappuccino add textured milk in different amounts and styles. A mocha adds chocolate and milk. Some cafés also serve espresso over ice or use it in cold milk drinks. The order may sound complicated, but the barista can listen for the drink base and the added parts. For example, a mocha needs espresso, chocolate, and milk. A long black needs espresso and water.

images.alt: English lesson illustration for Coffee Knowledge 1: Espresso Foundations scene 2: Several different black and milk coffee drinks show how one espresso base becomes many drinks.

items.prompt: What three parts are used in a mocha?
items.answer: A mocha uses espresso, chocolate, and milk.

blocks.title: 3. A Barista Does More Than Press a Button
paragraphs: Making espresso is only one part of a barista's work. A barista grinds coffee, checks the grinder, prepares the coffee in the basket, starts the shot, and tastes the result. The barista also textures milk, cleans the machine, keeps the work area safe, and manages customer orders. Coffee changes during the day. Heat, humidity, and the age of the beans can change how quickly a shot runs. For this reason, a barista watches the coffee and adjusts the grinder when needed. Good training teaches the worker how to notice a problem and make one careful change.

images.alt: English lesson illustration for Coffee Knowledge 1: Espresso Foundations scene 3: The trainee weighs, tamps, steams, and cleans at an organised coffee bench.

items.prompt: Why may a barista adjust the grinder during the day?
items.answer: Coffee and café conditions can change, so the shot may start running differently.

blocks.title: 4. Learn the House Recipe
paragraphs: Every café has a house recipe. The recipe tells the barista how much ground coffee to use, how much espresso to make, and how long the shot should take. It may also tell the worker how many shots go into each cup size. One café may use 18 grams of ground coffee. Another may use 20 or 22 grams. A large flat white may have two shots in one café and a different recipe in another. A new worker should not guess. The professional action is to ask, watch, measure, and follow the café's system.

images.alt: English lesson illustration for Coffee Knowledge 1: Espresso Foundations scene 4: The head barista teaches the trainee to measure and follow the cafe's house recipe.

items.prompt: Why should a new barista learn the house recipe?
items.answer: Coffee amounts, shot numbers, cup sizes, and drink methods can be different in each café.

blocks.title: Useful Speaking Patterns
paragraphs:
- How much ground coffee do you use here?
- How many shots go into this cup size?
- Could you show me one before I try?
It is Mia's first morning in an Australian café. She asks the head barista about the espresso recipe before making a flat white.

turns.speaker: Mia
turns.text: Good morning. I am ready to learn your espresso recipe.

turns.speaker: Head Barista
turns.text: Welcome, Mia. Let's start with the dose.

turns.speaker: Mia
turns.text: Thanks. How much ground coffee do you use here?

turns.speaker: Head Barista
turns.text: We use 20 grams and aim for 40 grams of espresso.

turns.speaker: Mia
turns.text: And how many shots go into a medium flat white?

turns.speaker: Head Barista
turns.text: We use two shots for that size.

turns.speaker: Mia
turns.text: Great. Could you show me one shot before I try?

turns.speaker: Head Barista
turns.text: Of course. Watch this one, and then you can make the next.

turns.speaker: Mia
turns.text: Thanks. I want to follow the house recipe correctly.

turns.speaker: Head Barista
turns.text: Good. Asking first is exactly the right thing to do.

turns.speaker: Mia
turns.text: Thank you. I am ready to start.

turns.speaker: Head Barista
turns.text: We will start together. See you there.

blocks.title: Final Reflection
paragraphs: Espresso is a brewing method and the base of many café drinks. A careful barista learns the whole process and follows the café's recipe. What is one question you would ask before making your first espresso at a new café?
